def: A purine base formed by deamination of adenine; it is the base in inosine and is salvaged back into IMP by HGPRT. Deficiency of HGPRT causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.

Lack of vitamin B1, a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and transketolase. Causes wet or dry beriberi and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, especially in alcohol use disorder.

Acute brain disease from thiamine deficiency, classically presenting with confusion, ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus, and ataxia. Treat with thiamine before glucose; untreated, it can progress to Korsakoff syndrome.

Vitamin B6, whose active form pyridoxal phosphate is a cofactor in transamination and neurotransmitter synthesis. Isoniazid causes deficiency, producing peripheral neuropathy and sideroblastic anemia.
Surgical removal of all or part of the stomach. It can cause vitamin B12 deficiency (loss of intrinsic factor), iron deficiency and dumping syndrome.
Ascending spinal pathways carrying unconscious proprioceptive information from muscles and joints to the cerebellum. They are damaged in Friedreich ataxia and vitamin E deficiency.

Autosomal dominant deficiency of porphobilinogen deaminase in heme synthesis. Attacks of abdominal pain, neuropsychiatric symptoms and dark urine, triggered by drugs, fasting or alcohol; no photosensitivity.
The most common porphyria, from deficient uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase. Causes blistering, fragile skin on sun-exposed areas; associated with hepatitis C, alcohol and iron overload.
Ring of tissue behind the iris that makes aqueous humor and contains the ciliary muscle controlling lens shape for accommodation.

term: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms
def: Delayed severe drug hypersensitivity with rash, fever, eosinophilia, lymphadenopathy and organ involvement (often liver), appearing weeks after starting a drug such as allopurinol, carbamazepine or sulfonamides.
syn: drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms

def: Antibody preparation, often from horses or humans, that neutralizes a bacterial toxin. Used for diphtheria, tetanus and botulism after exposure.
Upward movement of the big toe with fanning of the other toes when the sole is stroked. Normal in infants; in adults it indicates an upper motor neuron lesion.
Aggressive T-cell malignancy caused by HTLV-1 infection, endemic in Japan and the Caribbean. Features include hypercalcemia, skin lesions and lytic bone lesions, with characteristic flower cells.
Brainstem nuclei receiving sensation from the face via cranial nerve V: the main sensory nucleus (touch), spinal nucleus (pain and temperature) and mesencephalic nucleus (proprioception).
Brainstem nucleus extending into the upper cervical cord that receives pain and temperature from the face. Damage in lateral medullary syndrome causes ipsilateral facial numbness.
Thalamic relay nuclei: the lateral geniculate body relays visual input to the occipital cortex, and the medial geniculate body relays hearing to the auditory cortex.
The most abundant plasma protein, made by the liver. It maintains oncotic pressure and carries bilirubin, fatty acids, calcium and many drugs; low in liver disease and nephrotic syndrome.
Overgrowth of a single plasma cell clone producing one immunoglobulin (M protein). Includes MGUS, multiple myeloma and Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia.

Fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension and repetition, with the patient unaware of the errors. Caused by a lesion of the superior temporal gyrus (Wernicke area), usually from a middle cerebral artery stroke.
Almond-shaped limbic nucleus in the temporal lobe that processes fear and emotional memory. Bilateral damage causes Kluver-Bucy syndrome (hyperorality, hypersexuality, placidity).
A polyomavirus that stays latent in the kidneys and lymphoid tissue. In severely immunocompromised patients it reactivates to cause progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy.

Clot in a dural venous sinus, such as the sagittal or cavernous sinus, causing headache, seizures and venous infarction with hemorrhage. Linked to hypercoagulable states, pregnancy and oral contraceptives.
Misfolded, protease-resistant forms of the host protein PrP that convert normal PrP into more misfolded copies. They cause spongiform encephalopathies such as Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and kuru.

Malabsorption syndrome in people living in or visiting the tropics, with villous atrophy of the small intestine, probably after an infection. Causes folate and B12 deficiency; treated with antibiotics and folate.
Toxin of Vibrio cholerae that permanently activates Gs by ADP-ribosylation, raising cAMP in enterocytes. This causes chloride and water secretion and profuse rice-water diarrhea.
Congenital interruption of the esophagus, usually with a fistula to the trachea. Newborns drool, choke and cough with feeding; often part of VACTERL.
Outpouching of pharyngeal mucosa through Killian triangle above the upper esophageal sphincter. Causes dysphagia, halitosis and regurgitation of undigested food.

Chronic allergic inflammation of the esophagus with dense eosinophils, causing dysphagia and food impaction. Linked to atopy; shows rings or furrows on endoscopy and treated with PPIs, steroids or diet.

Branch of the aorta at L1 supplying the midgut, from the duodenum to the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon. Occlusion causes mesenteric ischemia; it can compress the duodenum in SMA syndrome.
The most common primary immunodeficiency, with absent serum IgA. Often asymptomatic or causes sinopulmonary and GI infections; anaphylaxis can occur with transfusions containing IgA.
Chinese liver fluke acquired by eating undercooked freshwater fish. Lives in bile ducts, causing cholangitis, pigmented gallstones and cholangiocarcinoma.
Sleep disorder of NREM slow-wave sleep in children with sudden screaming and autonomic arousal, but no recall the next morning. Usually resolves with age.
Excess endolymph in the inner ear, the pathology of Meniere disease. Causes episodic vertigo, low-frequency hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness.
Inner ear disorder from endolymphatic hydrops, with episodic vertigo lasting hours, fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and ear fullness.
Feeling of detachment from one's own body or mental processes, as if observing oneself from outside, with intact reality testing. Derealization is the same sense about the surroundings.
Infection of the CNS by Treponema pallidum, causing meningitis, tabes dorsalis or general paresis. Argyll Robertson pupils are classic; diagnosed by CSF VDRL and treated with IV penicillin.
Superficial skin infection by group A Streptococcus involving the upper dermis and lymphatics. Presents as a bright red, raised, sharply demarcated painful plaque, often on the face.
A long-acting benzodiazepine, used mainly to treat alcohol withdrawal. Enhances GABA-A receptor chloride channel opening frequency.
Brief electrical stimulation of the brain under anesthesia to induce a controlled seizure. Highly effective for severe depression, catatonia and mania; side effects include transient memory loss.
Psychiatric disorder of recurrent intrusive thoughts (obsessions) and repetitive behaviors (compulsions) that relieve distress. Treated with SSRIs and exposure and response prevention.
Peripheral DOPA decarboxylase inhibitor given with levodopa in Parkinson disease. It cannot cross the blood-brain barrier, so it reduces peripheral dopamine and side effects like nausea.

Reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that does not cross the blood-brain barrier. Used for myasthenia gravis, postoperative ileus and urinary retention, and to reverse nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockade.
Very short-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. Formerly used in the Tensilon test to diagnose myasthenia gravis, where it briefly improves muscle strength.
Bony outgrowth at joint margins formed in response to cartilage degeneration. Characteristic of osteoarthritis; at the DIP joints they are Heberden nodes.
Giving preformed antibodies, such as immunoglobulin or antitoxin, for immediate but short-lived protection. Used after exposures to rabies, hepatitis B, tetanus and botulism.

Immunosuppressant that binds FKBP and inhibits mTOR, blocking IL-2 signaling in T cells. Used in transplant rejection prophylaxis and drug-eluting stents; causes hyperlipidemia and impaired wound healing.

Hyper-IgE syndrome, usually from STAT3 mutation, with defective Th17 cells. Causes recurrent staphylococcal skin abscesses without inflammation (cold abscesses), eczema, retained baby teeth, coarse facies and high IgE.
Scar that grows beyond the original wound margins due to excess collagen (type III, later type I). More common in darker-skinned people, and it does not regress.
Oral direct thrombin inhibitor used for anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation and venous thromboembolism. Reversed by idarucizumab.
Oral anticoagulants (rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban) that directly block factor Xa. Used for atrial fibrillation and venous thromboembolism; reversed with andexanet alfa.
First-generation cephalosporin active against gram-positive cocci. Used for skin and soft tissue infections and uncomplicated urinary infections.
Inflammation of both the meninges and the brain tissue, causing fever, headache and altered mental status. Causes include viruses, Naegleria and Cryptococcus.
Bladder inflammation with bleeding, caused by cyclophosphamide or ifosfamide (acrolein metabolite), pelvic radiation, or adenovirus and BK virus. Mesna prevents the drug-induced form.
Injury to the radial nerve causing wrist drop and loss of finger and wrist extension. Caused by humeral shaft fracture, or sustained compression (Saturday night palsy).
Fainting from reflex vagal activation and sympathetic withdrawal, causing bradycardia and vasodilation. Triggered by pain, emotion or prolonged standing, often with prodromal nausea and sweating.
South American endemic fungal infection by Paracoccidioides, with a ship's wheel appearance of budding yeast. Causes lung disease and mucocutaneous ulcers.
Obligate intracellular bacterium transmitted by Dermacentor ticks that causes Rocky Mountain spotted fever. Infects vascular endothelium, causing vasculitis and a rash starting on wrists and ankles.
Small gram-negative intracellular coccobacillus acquired from unpasteurized dairy or livestock. Causes undulant fever, sweats and arthralgias (brucellosis).
Third-generation cephalosporin with activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Used for serious gram-negative infections such as in neutropenic fever.
Tick-borne illnesses from Rickettsia species (including Rocky Mountain spotted fever) causing fever, headache and rash. Treat with doxycycline.
Tick-borne Rickettsia rickettsii infection with fever, headache and a rash starting at wrists and ankles and spreading centrally, including palms and soles. Treat with doxycycline.
Systemic infection by Leishmania donovani from sandflies, with fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly and pancytopenia. Amastigotes are found in macrophages.
Free-living amoeba from warm fresh water that enters through the cribriform plate while swimming. Causes rapidly fatal primary amoebic meningoencephalitis.
Pinworm; a nematode causing perianal itching, especially at night. Diagnosed by the scotch tape test and treated with albendazole or pyrantel pamoate.
Antiparasitic that increases calcium permeability, causing paralysis of flukes and tapeworms. Used for schistosomiasis, liver flukes and cysticercosis.
Dog tapeworm that causes hydatid cysts, mainly in liver and lung, from sheep-herding contact. Cyst rupture can cause anaphylaxis.
Gram-negative bacterium causing typhoid (enteric) fever, with sustained fever, rose spots and relative bradycardia. Humans are the only reservoir; some become chronic gallbladder carriers.
Surgical removal of uterine fibroids while preserving the uterus. Chosen for symptomatic fibroids in women who want to retain fertility.
Motility disorder with uncoordinated, simultaneous esophageal contractions causing chest pain and dysphagia. Barium swallow shows a corkscrew esophagus; treated with calcium channel blockers.
Descent of pelvic organs into the vagina because of weakened pelvic floor support. Types include cystocele, rectocele and uterine prolapse.
High-risk HPV type that, with type 18, causes most cervical cancer. E6 inactivates p53 and E7 inactivates Rb.
Stain used on blood smears to detect malaria, Babesia, Trypanosoma and Borrelia, and to stain chromosomes (G-banding). Also identifies Chlamydia inclusions.
Membrane proteins that mediate fusion of vesicles with the plasma membrane for neurotransmitter release. Tetanus and botulinum toxins cleave them.
Mold in the order Mucorales causing mucormycosis, with broad, nonseptate hyphae branching at right angles. Seen in diabetic ketoacidosis and neutropenia, invading sinuses and brain.
Inflammation of the urethra with dysuria and discharge, most often from gonorrhea or chlamydia. Nongonococcal urethritis also includes Ureaplasma and Mycoplasma.
Colon inflammation from Clostridioides difficile toxins after antibiotics, with watery diarrhea and yellow-white pseudomembranes on colonoscopy. Treated with oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin.
Outer layer of the blastocyst forming the placenta. The inner cytotrophoblast is mitotic; the outer syncytiotrophoblast secretes hCG and invades the endometrium.
Innermost germ layer, forming the lining of the gut and respiratory tract, liver, pancreas, thyroid and bladder.
First fluid-filled structure of pregnancy seen on ultrasound within the uterus, around 4.5 to 5 weeks. Its absence with high hCG raises suspicion of ectopic pregnancy.
Chronic conjunctivitis from Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes A-C. Repeated infection causes follicles, scarring and inturned eyelashes (trichiasis); a leading infectious cause of blindness.
Common cause of anterior knee pain from abnormal patellar tracking, worse with stairs or sitting. Associated with a weak quadriceps and tight lateral structures.
Inner ear and central network that senses head position and motion for balance and gaze stability, using the semicircular canals and otolith organs.
Enzymes that bind and hydrolyze GTP to GDP, switching between active and inactive states. Include G proteins and Ras.
Enzyme converting GTP to cGMP. It mediates nitric oxide and ANP signaling, causing smooth muscle relaxation.
Lack of secondary sex characteristics by age 13 in girls or 14 in boys. Causes include constitutional delay, hypogonadism, Turner and Kallmann syndromes.
Outermost adrenal cortex layer that makes aldosterone under control of angiotensin II and potassium.
Excess calcium in the urine, the most common cause of kidney stones. Seen with hypercalcemia, loop diuretics and idiopathic causes; treated with thiazides.
Vitamin D3, made in skin by UV light or taken from animal foods. Hydroxylated in liver and then kidney to active calcitriol.
Test where blood glucose is measured two hours after a 75 g glucose load. A level of 200 mg/dL or higher diagnoses diabetes; also used to screen for gestational diabetes.
Reversible nonselective alpha-adrenergic blocker. Used for pheochromocytoma crises, extravasation of norepinephrine and cocaine-induced hypertension.
Cells in spermatogenesis: primary spermatocytes are diploid and enter meiosis I, giving haploid secondary spermatocytes that divide to spermatids.
Oral diabetes drugs (sitagliptin, linagliptin) that block breakdown of GLP-1 and GIP, raising insulin and lowering glucagon. Weight neutral; rare pancreatitis.

Peptide co-secreted with insulin by pancreatic beta cells that slows gastric emptying and suppresses glucagon. Its deposits form islet amyloid in type 2 diabetes; analog pramlintide is used therapeutically.
Embryonic duct that in males becomes the epididymis, vas deferens and seminal vesicles under testosterone. Regresses in females.
Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor that raises cGMP and relaxes smooth muscle. Used for erectile dysfunction and pulmonary hypertension; contraindicated with nitrates.
Synthetic androgen that suppresses gonadotropin release. Used for endometriosis and hereditary angioedema; side effects include virilization and hepatotoxicity.
Malignant ovarian germ cell tumor, the female counterpart of seminoma. Sheets of uniform cells with clear cytoplasm; elevated LDH and radiosensitive.
Ovarian tumors from sex cord or stromal cells, including granulosa cell, Sertoli-Leydig, thecoma and fibroma. Often secrete hormones.
Sexually transmitted infection by Chlamydia trachomatis L1-L3. Causes a painless ulcer followed by painful inguinal lymphadenopathy (buboes) and possible rectal stricture.
Surgical fixation of an undescended testis into the scrotum, ideally by 6-12 months. Reduces infertility and torsion risk.
Embryonic connection between the midgut and yolk sac. Persistence causes Meckel diverticulum, or rarely a fistula.
Plasma glycoprotein that binds platelets to damaged endothelium and carries factor VIII. Deficiency causes von Willebrand disease; activity measured by ristocetin cofactor assay.
Prenatal diagnostic test removing placental villi at 10-13 weeks for karyotype or DNA testing. Earlier than amniocentesis but carries a small risk of limb defects and miscarriage.
Synthetic corticosteroid with strong mineralocorticoid effect. Given for adrenal insufficiency and orthostatic hypotension to retain sodium and water.
Family of receptor tyrosine kinases (EGFR, HER2 and others). Overexpression drives cancer, targeted by trastuzumab, cetuximab and erlotinib.
Repair pathway that fixes base mismatches and small loops after DNA replication. Defects cause Lynch syndrome and microsatellite instability.
Exotoxin of Corynebacterium diphtheriae that ADP-ribosylates elongation factor 2, halting protein synthesis. Causes pharyngeal pseudomembranes and myocarditis.
Compounds with a sugar attached to a non-sugar group. Medical examples include cardiac glycosides, like digoxin, and anthraquinone laxatives.
Drugs such as digoxin that block the Na+/K+ ATPase, raising intracellular calcium and increasing contractility. Toxicity causes nausea, yellow vision and arrhythmias.
Collagen forming the sheet-like network of basement membranes. Defects cause Alport syndrome; autoantibodies cause Goodpasture syndrome.
Vitamin C deficiency impairing collagen hydroxylation. Causes bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhages, poor wound healing and corkscrew hairs.
X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder from MECP2 mutation, affecting girls. After normal early development, loss of speech and purposeful hand use with hand-wringing, and microcephaly.
Drug that inhibits the funny current (If) in the sinoatrial node, lowering heart rate without reducing contractility. Used in chronic heart failure and angina.
Voltage-gated calcium channels in cardiac and smooth muscle. In skeletal muscle they function as dihydropyridine receptors; dihydropyridine drugs block them.
Delayed conduction in the left or right bundle branch, widening the QRS above 120 ms. RBBB shows rSR' in V1; LBBB shows a broad notched R in V6.
Biologic drugs (infliximab, adalimumab, etanercept) that block tumor necrosis factor. Used in rheumatoid arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease; raise risk of TB reactivation.
Net-like violaceous mottling of the skin from sluggish cutaneous blood flow. Seen with cold exposure, vasculitis, antiphospholipid syndrome and cholesterol emboli.
Reversal of a left-to-right shunt into right-to-left shunt as pulmonary hypertension rises. Causes late cyanosis, clubbing and polycythemia.
Injection of local anesthetic around a nerve to cause regional numbness. Used for surgery or pain control.
Benign tumor of primitive connective tissue, most commonly the left atrial cardiac myxoma. Gelatinous mass causing a "tumor plop" and embolic or obstructive symptoms.
Class III antiarrhythmic with beta blocking properties. Blocks potassium channels and prolongs the QT interval, risking torsades de pointes.
Structural protein of chylomicrons, made in the intestine from the same gene as B-100 through RNA editing. Needed to export dietary fat; absent in abetalipoproteinemia.
Hemoglobin with two alpha and two gamma chains (HbF). Has higher oxygen affinity than adult hemoglobin because it binds 2,3-BPG less. Hydroxyurea raises HbF in sickle cell disease.
Immediate IgE-mediated allergic reaction in which allergen cross-links IgE on mast cells and basophils. Causes anaphylaxis, asthma and urticaria.
Pneumoconiosis from inhaling silica in mining or sandblasting. Upper-lobe nodules with eggshell calcification of hilar nodes; raises TB and cancer risk.
Chronic granulomatous lung disease from beryllium exposure in aerospace and electronics work. Resembles sarcoidosis, with noncaseating granulomas.
Pneumoconiosis from asbestos exposure causing lower-lobe interstitial fibrosis and pleural plaques. Increases risk of lung cancer and mesothelioma; ferruginous bodies seen.
Apical lung cancer invading the brachial plexus and sympathetic chain. Causes arm pain and Horner syndrome (miosis, ptosis, anhidrosis).
Absence (or reduced, hypohidrosis) of sweating. Seen in Horner syndrome, ectodermal dysplasia and with anticholinergic drugs.
Inherited platelet disorder from GPIb deficiency, impairing adhesion to von Willebrand factor. Giant platelets and mucocutaneous bleeding.
Inherited platelet disorder from deficiency of GpIIb/IIIa, impairing aggregation. Normal platelet count and abnormal bleeding with no ristocetin-independent aggregation.
Enzyme that phosphorylates galactose to galactose-1-phosphate. Deficiency causes mild galactosemia with infantile cataracts, but no liver damage.
Cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase. Sometimes used as an antioxidant.
Membrane transport protein that moves two substances in opposite directions, such as the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger.
Mitochondrial enzyme converting pyruvate to oxaloacetate, requiring biotin and ATP. Important in gluconeogenesis; activated by acetyl-CoA.
Intermediate in transsulfuration formed from homocysteine and serine by cystathionine beta-synthase. Deficiency causes homocystinuria.
Blood clot in veins, including deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. Risk from stasis, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability (Virchow triad).
Inhaled or intranasal corticosteroid used in asthma and allergic rhinitis. Can cause oral thrush.
Intestinal obstruction in a newborn from thick meconium in the ileum. Strongly associated with cystic fibrosis.
Serine proteases; plasma kallikrein converts kininogen to bradykinin. Implicated in hereditary angioedema.
Funnel-shaped collecting structure of the kidney that receives urine from the calyces and drains into the ureter. Site of pyelonephritis and transitional cell cancers.
Drugs that block adrenergic receptors; include alpha blockers and beta blockers.
Membrane ATPase pumping protons across membranes. Gastric parietal cells use H+/K+ ATPase to secrete acid; PPIs block it.
Presence of immunoglobulins that precipitate in the cold. Causes vasculitis with palpable purpura, arthralgia and glomerulonephritis; associated with hepatitis C.
Selective alpha-1A blocker used for benign prostatic hyperplasia. Relaxes prostate and bladder neck smooth muscle; can cause orthostatic hypotension and floppy iris syndrome.
Specialized ependymal tissue in the ventricles that produces cerebrospinal fluid.
Damage to the inner ear from drugs, causing hearing loss and balance problems. Causes include aminoglycosides, loop diuretics, cisplatin and aspirin.
Mitochondrial enzymes catalyzing the first step of beta oxidation. Medium-chain deficiency (MCAD) causes hypoketotic hypoglycemia.
Glycolipids with sialic acid abundant in neuronal membranes. Accumulate in Tay-Sachs and Sandhoff diseases.
X-linked alpha-galactosidase A deficiency causing glycolipid accumulation. Presents with angiokeratomas, burning pain in the extremities, corneal opacities and kidney and heart failure.
Autosomal recessive galactocerebrosidase deficiency. Causes peripheral neuropathy, optic atrophy, globoid cells and developmental delay.
Inflammation of the cornea. Causes include herpes simplex and contact lens infection; presents with pain and photophobia.
Oral vitamin A derivative for severe acne. Highly teratogenic; also causes dry skin and hypertriglyceridemia.
First committed precursor of heme, made by ALA synthase from glycine and succinyl-CoA. Accumulates in lead poisoning and porphyrias.
Sudden, rapid, repetitive, nonrhythmic movements or sounds that can be briefly suppressed. Seen in Tourette syndrome.
Amine from fermented foods that causes norepinephrine release. With MAOIs it can precipitate hypertensive crisis.
Selective beta-1 blocker used mainly as eye drops for glaucoma to reduce aqueous humor production.
Common postural/kinetic tremor of the hands, often familial. Improves with alcohol; treated with propranolol or primidone.
Intracellular protozoan transmitted by Ixodes ticks that infects red blood cells. Causes hemolytic anemia; smear shows ring forms and Maltese cross.
Autonomic nerves to abdominal organs. Thoracic splanchnic nerves are preganglionic sympathetic; pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-4) are parasympathetic.
Neurodegenerative disease of upper and lower motor neurons. Causes progressive weakness, atrophy and fasciculations with preserved sensation; riluzole slows progression.
Vertebral arch defect with an intact spinal cord and no protrusion. Often has a tuft of hair or dimple over the lumbosacral area.
B-cell precursors in bone marrow that rearrange heavy chain genes and express the pre-B cell receptor. Absent in Bruton agammaglobulinemia.
Cranial nerve XI, which supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. Injury causes shoulder droop and weak head turning.
Cranial nerve XII, which supplies the tongue muscles. Injury causes tongue deviation toward the lesion.
Three fluid-filled loops of the inner ear detecting rotational head movement through cupula deflection. BPPV is caused by debris here.
Fluid-filled space between the cornea and iris containing aqueous humor. Its angle is the site of drainage; blockage causes angle-closure glaucoma.
Inflammation of the optic nerve causing painful monocular vision loss and a relative afferent pupillary defect. Associated with multiple sclerosis.
B-cell lymphoma from t(11;14), causing cyclin D1 overexpression. CD5-positive; involves lymph nodes and the gut.
Region in the inferior frontal gyrus controlling speech production. Damage causes Broca aphasia.
Superior temporal gyrus region responsible for language comprehension. Damage causes Wernicke aphasia.
Non-fluent speech with intact comprehension and impaired repetition; patient is aware of difficulty. Caused by damage to the inferior frontal gyrus.
Enterovirus in the picornavirus group causing aseptic meningitis, rash and gastroenteritis. Transmitted by the fecal-oral route.
Mosquito-borne flavivirus with bird reservoirs. Usually mild febrile illness; can cause meningoencephalitis and flaccid paralysis.
Slowness of movement and difficulty initiating movement, a core feature of Parkinson disease.
Tumor of glial cells, including astrocytomas, oligodendrogliomas and ependymomas. Glioblastoma is the most aggressive.
Autosomal dominant NF2 mutation causing bilateral vestibular schwannomas, meningiomas and ependymomas. Hearing loss and tinnitus are early symptoms.
Distal stomach segment ending in the pyloric sphincter, which controls emptying into the duodenum. Hypertrophy causes projectile vomiting in infants.
Functional bowel disorder with abdominal pain related to defecation and altered bowel habits, without structural disease.
Endoscopic exam of the rectum and sigmoid colon used for screening and evaluating lower GI bleeding.
Duct draining the gallbladder, joining the common hepatic duct to form the common bile duct. Gallstone obstruction causes cholecystitis.
Immune cross-reaction in which antibodies to a microbe attack similar host antigens. Seen in rheumatic fever and Guillain-Barre syndrome.
Long-acting benzodiazepine used for panic disorder, seizures and REM sleep behavior disorder.
Enzyme that converts fibrinogen to fibrin, which Staphylococcus aureus produces; positive coagulase test distinguishes S aureus from other staphylococci.
Bacterial enzymes that cross-link peptidoglycan in cell walls. Beta-lactams bind them; altered PBP2a in MRSA confers resistance.
Depolarizing neuromuscular blocker with rapid onset. Risks include hyperkalemia and malignant hyperthermia.
SSRI used for depression and OCD. Has a long half-life and risk of serotonin syndrome.
SNRI for depression and anxiety. May cause hypertension.
